Detection.step: Confirm the alert details — source IP, target account, event count and timeframe
Verify source IP is NOT an authorized scanner (check scanner IP whitelist: Nessus, Qualys, red team ranges)
Check if ANY login attempt succeeded — search for Event 4624 from the same source IP after the 4625 cluster

Triage.step: Identify the targeted account — is it admin, service account, or regular user?
Check geo-location and ASN of source IP — is it expected for this user?
Review MFA status on the targeted account in Active Directory
Determine if this is an isolated incident or part of a wider campaign (same IP attacking multiple accounts?)

Containment.step: [SIMULATED] Block source IP at perimeter firewall — confirm with network team before executing on production
Temporarily lock the targeted account if a successful login is confirmed
Force password reset on the account if compromise is suspected

Eradication.step: Reset compromised credentials and invalidate active sessions
Verify MFA is enabled and functioning on the account
Review account for unauthorized changes made during the compromised session

Recovery.step: Monitor account activity for 48 hours for continued suspicious behavior
Document all IOCs (source IP, targeted accounts, timestamps)
Update detection rule threshold if alert was a false positive (tune for scanner IPs)

Detection.step: Capture the full command line including the -EncodedCommand value
Identify the parent process that launched PowerShell — document the full parent path

Triage.step: Classify parent process — is it Office (phishing macro), browser (drive-by), or scheduled task (persistence)?
List all child processes spawned by the PowerShell process (Sysmon Event 1, parent PID filter)
Check all outbound network connections from the PowerShell process (Sysmon Event 3)
Search destination IP/domain in local threat intel — is it known malicious?
Check file creation events (Sysmon Event 11) from the PowerShell process — was a payload dropped?

Containment.step: [SIMULATED] Isolate the affected endpoint from the network
[SIMULATED] Block destination IP/domain at firewall and DNS filter
Terminate the malicious PowerShell process if still running

Eradication.step: Search for and remove any dropped payload files (use file hash to search across environment)
Check registry run keys for persistence (HKLM/HKCU\CurrentVersion\Run)
Submit file hash and decoded command to sandbox for analysis
Search same IOCs (hash, IP, domain) across all other endpoints

Recovery.step: Restore endpoint from backup or reimage if malware infection confirmed
Enable PowerShell Script Block Logging (Event 4104) if not already enabled
Consider enforcing PowerShell Constrained Language Mode for standard users
Document decoded command, IOCs, and attack chain in incident report

PB-PROC-001.title: Malicious Office Child Process Response Playbook

Detection.step: Identify the Office application and document that triggered the child process spawn
Determine the full command line of the spawned child process
Check the document origin — email attachment, download, shared drive?

Triage.step: Verify with the user — did they intentionally open this document and enable macros?
Check email headers if document came as attachment — is sender spoofed or external?
List all subsequent processes in the chain (child, grandchild) using PID tracking
Review network connections from child processes — was data exfiltrated or C2 contacted?

Containment.step: Quarantine the malicious document — preserve for forensic analysis
[SIMULATED] Block communication to identified C2 addresses

Eradication.step: Remove any payload files dropped by the macro execution
Check for persistence mechanisms added during execution (registry, scheduled tasks, startup)
Submit document and payload hashes to sandbox/AV
Search document hash and IOCs across all endpoints

Recovery.step: Restore endpoint to known-good state if malware executed successfully
Report phishing email to email security team for sender domain/IP blocking
Disable macros by default via Group Policy for non-authorized users
Conduct user awareness training on document-based phishing

Detection.step: Confirm scan source IP and total ports scanned within the time window
Check scanner IP against authorized scanner whitelist (Nessus, Qualys, red team IPs)
Determine if scan is from internal network (lateral movement concern) or external

Triage.step: Identify which internal hosts were scanned — any critical assets targeted?
Check if scanner subsequently attempted to authenticate to discovered open ports
Review firewall logs for same source IP in the preceding 24 hours

Containment.step: [SIMULATED] Block source IP at perimeter firewall if unauthorized
Null-route the source IP at network level if internal scan from compromised host
Alert network team to increase monitoring on the scanned IP range

Eradication.step: If internal source: investigate the scanning host for compromise (malware, unauthorized tool)
Review and tighten firewall rules based on what was discovered to be open

Recovery.step: Monitor for follow-up exploitation attempts on ports that were found open
Document scan scope, source, and classification (authorized/unauthorized)
If false positive: add scanner IP to whitelist and tune alert suppression

Detection.step: Identify the account that received the sensitive privileges (Event 4672 Subject Account)
Confirm this is NOT a service account or admin tool that legitimately requires these privileges
Check Event 4673 (Privileged Service Called) correlated with the same logon ID

Triage.step: Review Sysmon Event 10 (ProcessAccess) for LSASS access from non-system processes on this host
List all processes created during the elevated session (Event 4688 filtered by logon ID)
Check for whoami.exe, mimikatz.exe, or similar credential-dumping tools in process list
Determine if credentials were exfiltrated — check network connections from elevated session

Containment.step: [SIMULATED] Isolate the affected endpoint from the network
Invalidate the active session token — force re-authentication
Lock the affected account pending investigation

Eradication.step: If credential dump confirmed: initiate domain-wide password reset for all accounts
Rotate service account credentials and Kerberos tickets (krbtgt reset if necessary)
Remove any tools or payloads used to obtain the elevated token

Recovery.step: Enable Windows Credential Guard on affected and at-risk endpoints
Apply principle of least privilege — audit accounts with SeDebugPrivilege
Monitor for lateral movement using credentials obtained during the incident

Detection.step: Capture the exact registry key path, value name, and value data (executable path)
Identify the process that wrote the registry key (should be msiexec.exe or installer — if cmd/powershell, high confidence malicious)
Verify the referenced executable exists on disk and retrieve its hash

Triage.step: Check executable hash against AV/threat intel — is it known malware?
Compare against IT asset inventory — is this a known-good application?
Trace back how the executable was delivered — check recent file creation events on the host
Check if executable has already executed (look for child processes of that executable)

Containment.step: [SIMULATED] Remove the malicious registry run key entry
Prevent the executable from running via AppLocker or hash block rule

Eradication.step: Search for additional persistence mechanisms on the same host (scheduled tasks, startup folder, services)
Search for the same executable hash across all endpoints in the environment
Trace the initial access vector that delivered the malware

Recovery.step: Reimage endpoint if malware has been active for an extended period
Implement registry monitoring and baselining for run key paths on all endpoints
Document the persistence mechanism, IOCs, and remediation in the incident report
